headline: SNDL's Atholville wins EU-GMP as Rubicon opens a genetics site
dek: SNDL's New Brunswick grow is now certified to supply Europe's medical markets, and Rubicon Organics has a federal licence for a genetics hub in Squamish.
key_points: SNDL's Atholville, New Brunswick facility received EU-GMP certification on 4 November for producing and packaging medical cannabis flower.
The site can produce about 4,500 kg a quarter and SNDL says it could exceed 30 tonnes a year with more investment; lighting upgrades are under way.
Rubicon Organics' Arbora site in Squamish, BC, was listed by Health Canada on 6 November as a micro-cultivation licence and will house 500+ cultivars.
Both moves aim at the same thing: higher-value product for export and premium shelves as Canadian wholesale prices stay weak.
body: Two Canadian producers moved to strengthen their position at the top end of the market this week. SNDL said its Atholville, New Brunswick cultivation site has received European Union Good Manufacturing Practice certification, and Rubicon Organics announced a federally licensed genetics facility in Squamish, British Columbia, StratCann reported on 9 November.

EU-GMP certification is the standard most European medical markets require for imported cannabis. Rubicon's move is aimed at the other half of premium: owning distinctive genetics that competitors cannot easily copy.

SNDL said the certification was granted on 4 November and covers the production and packaging of cannabis flower for regulated medical markets. The company completed the audit on 4 August and said then that it expected certification within 90 days, so the approval arrived roughly on schedule. Chief executive Zachary George said lighting upgrades are now under way at the site.

Atholville, formerly owned by Zenabis, covers about 380,000 square feet with more than 110,000 square feet of canopy. SNDL puts its current capacity at about 4,500 kilograms a quarter, roughly 18 tonnes a year, and says targeted investment could take it beyond 30 tonnes. International sales are still small for SNDL: they rose from $3.8 million in the second quarter of 2025 to $5 million a year later, StratCann reported, an increase of about 32%.

The certification lands in the middle of a strategic review. As we reported on 6 November, SNDL's cannabis operations segment posted falling revenue and a negative gross margin in the third quarter, and management is reviewing the production business, with the CFO saying all options are valid. An EU-GMP site with room to grow is a more saleable, or more exportable, asset than one without it.

Cultivation is a small part of SNDL's story. The Edmonton-based company is Canada's largest private-sector liquor and cannabis retailer, with banners including Value Buds, Spiritleaf, Cost Cannabis, Ace Liquor and Wine and Beyond. It reported net revenue of $238 million in the third quarter, with gross profit of $57.9 million and a net loss of $50.8 million, StratCann noted.
> For SNDL, Atholville's certificate is worth as much in a sale process as on an export invoice. Either way, it puts a price on a grow the company has been questioning.
## Rubicon builds a home for its library

Rubicon Organics said its new facility, Arbora, is a leased site in Squamish that has received a federal licence to cultivate. Health Canada's public licence table lists Rubicon Holdings Corp. (3rd site) as a micro-cultivation licensee from 6 November, authorised to sell plants and seeds to provincial distributors and retailers. It will be used to preserve, propagate and develop the company's library of more than 500 cultivars.

Chief executive Margaret Brodie called the genetics library one of the company's most important strategic assets. Rubicon, a certified organic producer whose brands include Simply Bare Organics, 1964 Supply Co., Wildflower and Homestead Cannabis Supply, already runs a 125,000-square-foot facility in Delta, BC, and a 47,500-square-foot indoor site in Hope, BC. It reports third-quarter results before the market opens on 16 November.

Rubicon is not alone in investing in breeding. StratCann lists dedicated genetics or nursery operations at several Canadian producers, including Aurora's Aurora Coast research and breeding facility on Vancouver Island, a site that would pass to Organigram if its takeover of Aurora is approved.

The library already feeds Rubicon's shelves. Recent releases include BC Organic Lemolada and BC Organic Mandarin Zktz in early 2026, and Caviar Z under the Simply Bare premium brand. Other Canadian companies with dedicated breeding or nursery sites include Klonetics Plant Science, now part of Segra International, Trichome Hills in Ontario and Cannara Biotech in Quebec.

Canadian producers are leaning on exports because the domestic wholesale market is under pressure. As we reported on 9 November, Village Farms grew international sales 75% in the third quarter while its cannabis margin fell on weak Canadian trim prices. Germany is the biggest pull: it imported 205 tonnes of medical cannabis in 2025, with Canada supplying 46%, according to federal BfArM data compiled by Business of Cannabis.

Watch for SNDL to name export partners or destination markets for Atholville flower, and for any outcome of its production review. Rubicon reports on 16 November; listen for how much revenue its premium genetics bring and whether it plans export sales of its own.
